questions.question: What is population density?
choices: Population divided by land area
Land area divided by total exports
Births divided by deaths
Total population divided by average income

questions.question: What is a census?
choices: A survey of weather patterns only
A map of national elevation
An official count and collection of population information
An estimate of mineral reserves only

questions.question: What is natural population increase?
choices: Immigration minus emigration
Births minus deaths
Total population minus land area
Exports minus imports

questions.question: What is net migration?
choices: Births minus deaths
Population divided by area
The number of children per household
Immigration minus emigration

questions.question: What does a population pyramid show?
choices: Population by age and sex categories
The height of buildings by district
Only migration routes
Only national income levels

questions.question: What is life expectancy?
choices: The age of the oldest living person
The number of births in one year
Expected years of life based on mortality conditions
The average age at first migration

questions.question: What is fertility rate commonly used to measure?
choices: The number of deaths per square kilometer
Average births per woman under specified demographic conditions
The annual number of emigrants
The share of income spent on food

questions.question: Why does population density alone not show how people are distributed?
choices: Every region has uniform settlement
Density measures only total births
Land area has no effect on density
People may cluster unevenly within a region

questions.question: Why can a population grow even when its birth rate falls?
choices: Births may still exceed deaths, and migration may add residents
Falling birth rates always mean immediate population decline
Death rates cannot change
Migration never affects population size

questions.question: What change often accompanies early stages of the demographic transition?
choices: Birth and death rates both become zero
Migration stops permanently
Death rates decline before birth rates decline substantially
Every person moves to a city immediately

questions.question: Why can improved sanitation increase population growth initially?
choices: Sanitation necessarily raises birth rates by the same amount
Lower mortality can widen the gap between births and deaths
Sanitation makes emigration impossible
Lower mortality reduces the number of surviving children

questions.question: What does a broad base on a population pyramid often indicate?
choices: An absence of young residents
A population composed mainly of retirees
Identical population counts in every age group
A large share of children and recent high birth rates

questions.question: Why can an aging population create policy challenges?
choices: Demand for pensions and health services may rise relative to the working-age population
Older residents never contribute to society
Aging eliminates demand for health care
The number of workers must automatically double

questions.question: Why can rapid city growth pressure infrastructure?
choices: Cities have unlimited water supplies by definition
Population growth removes the need for schools
Housing, transport, and services may not expand as quickly as population
Infrastructure adjusts instantly without investment

questions.question: Why should demographic models be applied cautiously?
choices: Models make observation unnecessary
Countries' histories and conditions do not follow one identical path
Every country's population changes at the same rate
Migration has no effect on demographic patterns

questions.question: A region has 1 million residents and 10,000 square kilometers of land. What is its population density?
choices: 10 people per square kilometer
1,000 people per square kilometer
10,000 people per square kilometer
100 people per square kilometer

questions.question: A country records 500,000 births and 300,000 deaths, with no migration. What is its natural increase?
choices: 200,000 people
800,000 people
300,000 people
500,000 people

questions.question: A city gains 20,000 immigrants and loses 12,000 emigrants. What is its net migration?
choices: 32,000 people
12,000 people
8,000 people
20,000 people

questions.question: Two countries have equal population totals but one has half the land area. How do their average densities compare?
choices: The smaller country has half the density
The smaller country has twice the density
They necessarily have equal density
Their densities cannot be compared using these data

questions.question: A large young generation enters childbearing ages even as fertility declines. What process can sustain growth?
choices: Complete demographic decline
Negative net migration alone
A decrease in the number of potential parents
Population momentum
